US EXCEPTIONALISM was supposed to be last year's theme. This year was expected to be all about balance and broadening of growth across countries. That vision has not quite played out.

From an economic point of view, the US continues to outpace other major economies. The significant gap in artificial‑intelligence capital spending is believed to be one of the main reasons for this divergence.

The market has put US' AI capital expenditure this year at an estimated US$800 billion, whereas China's is only about US$100 billion, and Europe's AI‑related spending is roughly 5 per cent of the US level.

The primary beneficiary of the AI capex boom has been emerging market technology hardware and semiconductor stocks, particularly in South Korea. At their peak this year, MSCI Emerging Markets Information Technology Index had advanced over 100 per cent from January.

The South Korea segment of the index was up around 250 per cent. Even after the large correction from late June, the stocks are still up about 80 per cent in aggregate as at Sep 8, 2026, after the summer correction on the back of worries around the ability of hyperscalers to monetise the immense capital invested.

US hardware stocks have led the summer sell-off, which has spilled over into Asia. If US technology capex cools down, it is likely to trigger a synchronised correction, as the building of compute capacity is interconnected with Asia via the supply chains.

What goes up must come down?

The dramatic drop in tech stocks has understandably raised questions about whether the AI bubble is bursting. Investors are demanding clearer evidence of return on investment, as operating costs may outpace broader AI commercialisation efforts.

In Korea, investor leverage and leveraged exchange-traded funds have exacerbated the swings in the market.

That said, the concerns over immense capex deployed into AI and the ability of the hyperscalers to generate revenues have eased, with the release of strong Q2 earnings. Importantly we have seen signs of monetisation, as enterprise adoption of AI in diverse spheres is taking shape.

Some market players see valuations as a concern, but such a view is not supported by data. At late June's market peak, the MSCI Korea Technology Hardware & Equipment Index's forward price-earnings ratio was just 7.2 times compared to a long-run average of 12.5 times. That is, P/Es were below average even then and are lower now.

Hence, the valuations do not seem to be stretched. Notably, 2026 earnings-per-share estimates for the largest Korean hardware and semiconductor stocks have been going up. We are of the view that the summer sell-off was more technical than fundamentally driven.

Overall, hardware tech stocks appear to have simply corrected after an oversized rally. Their growth outlook remains solid. By contrast, software companies face challenges from AI, while the hyperscalers see short‑term earnings pressure from their massive capex programmes.

title: Is there a bubble in tech stocks? Summer sell-off was more technical than fundamental

Chevron is getting a sweet deal on Venezuela's sour crude.

Last week, the Houston-based company announced that it's investing more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years, more than doubling its production there to roughly 600,000 barrels a day. Chevron is already the largest private oil producer in the South American country, where it has been operating since 1923, meaning it has plenty of experience and the right infrastructure to make the most of the expansion. The company's three joint ventures in Venezuela have grown production by 15% year-to-date, and the new agreement comes with "enhanced fiscal, commercial and legal terms" plus more acreage in the Orinoco Belt, per the statement. Total costs will be less than $20 per barrel.

Oil Economics

Venezuela has the world's largest oil reserves, but its energy industry isn't close to taking full advantage of that potential. Reuters reports that its current oil output is only about 1.25 million barrels per day (bpd) compared with the more than 3 million bpd it was producing 20 years ago. The decline is the result of dysfunction at PDVSA, its state-run oil firm. But US Energy Secretary Chris Wright recently said that the country is expected to hit 2 million bpd by the end of the decade.

It'll take years before Chevron hits the numbers outlined in the deal, and even when it does, it won't be bringing enough online to replace Persian Gulf crude. But there's plenty untapped, and the US is looking to take advantage:

* GE Vernova recently agreed to help fix portions of the country's power grid. The Department of Energy says it "plans to bring 1 gigawatt of new reliable power online within the first 24 months, in addition to 5 gigawatts over the following four years, significantly expanding Venezuela's power capacity." Wright recently traveled to Venezuela to oversee the closure of the deals with Chevron, GE Vernova and Italian energy company Eni.

* Chevron's news came just days after President Trump announced a separate (and unusual) deal to take control of a large portion of Venezuela's oil reserves via a partnership with a private company.

Crude Awakening: The Chevron deal points to the broader dislocation in the energy markets that continues to be top of mind for policymakers and investors. As geopolitical risks interrupt traditional supply routes, it's becoming more important to tap into areas with major reserves, even if it will take billions of dollars and years to turn investments into actual energy security.

Investor concerns about Oracle center on spending and debt. The evidence to justify them is easier to spot than a California transplant in Austin, where the company is headquartered.

Oracle's June earnings release revealed negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in the 2026 fiscal year. Did Washington County just roll out the red carpet for constructing data centers?

Several seemingly unrelated events indicate we have. Starting with Ozarks Electric's plan to terminate its 77-year relationship with the Arkansas Electric Cooperative Corp. Ozarks plans to go independent so they can shop around for electrical capacity. Seems a bit like selling a good milk cow so you can go to the store and buy milk by the gallon. The letter I got from Ozarks as a member claims they need the flexibility to make "plans." Color me curious about modifying an agreement that's served Northwest Arkansas well since 1949.

And consider this, too. Last fall the Quorum Court agreed to issue $485 million in revenue bonds to provide upgrades for Ozark's local grid and communications systems. These investments target industrial expansion. Also this summer the Quorum Court declared a PACE district (Property Assessed Capital Expenditures) giving businesses access to cheap capital for energy efficiency and water conservation. These are all good ideas: utility innovation, public-

private partnerships and improving business infrastructure. However the convergence with the speculative AI bubble in the financial markets seems more than a coincidence. Color me worried that we are ripe for the picking.

Two other factors that the billionaires and hyper-scalers need to construct a data center: water and weak regulations. Water is plentiful for now. With regard to government oversight, just ask my Tontitown neighbors how their landfill-adjacent health concerns have been received by the Arkansas Division of Environmental Quality and the Quorum Court. Color me urgent to get in front of data centers.

Washington County needs to develop strong zoning and environmental regulations that give us a fighting chance to control our destiny. A moratorium on large-scale projects that consume gigawatts of electricity without creating ongoing jobs is a good start.

Let's roll up the red carpet and figure this out.

MAC MAYFIELD

Fayetteville

For sake of nation,

head to the streets

ASML, TSMC, Samsung and Intel just told the entire chip industry how AI processors will get made for the next seven years, and it starts with photomasks four times the size of today's.

Four companies control nearly every advanced chip on earth. On September 8th they laid out where that supply chain is headed. ASML and TSMC announced a joint initiative to move the industry from today's 6-inch photomasks, the templates that etch circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, to a new 12-inch format. Samsung joined the same day, expanding its existing partnership with the Dutch lithography maker. Intel is already running the machines the plan depends on.

The numbers, laid out in a joint statement carried by GlobeNewswire, are specific. The group is targeting a 12-inch mask pilot line by 2031, with 12-inch High-NA EUV lithography systems entering advanced-node production by 2033. Samsung will bring ASML's High-NA EUV machines into high-volume manufacturing by 2028, starting with DRAM. TSMC follows in 2030. Each machine runs about $400 million, according to Bloomberg's reporting on the announcement.

Four hundred million dollars. For one machine.

Intel got there first. The company has already run more than a million wafers through its High-NA EUV tools, according to Tom's Hardware - more than the rest of the industry combined. It's also the company trailblazing the larger 6x12 photomasks the new initiative depends on. For years, that looked like a lonely, expensive gamble. TSMC and Samsung waited. Now the other two are committing to the same machines, on their own timelines but the same technology.

TSMC posts record revenue and hands Wall Street its verdict on the AI buildout

TSMC reported record second-quarter revenue of about $39.62 billion on Thursday, a print Wall Street is treating as a referendum on the entire AI infrastructure trade after chip stocks lost well over a trillion dollars in value since June. Sold-out CoWoS packaging capacity and ASML's second straight guidance raise suggest the demand behind the... - TSMC record revenue AI spending - whether AI bubble is real

The Stencil Problem

You can think of a photomask as the stencil a fab uses to print a chip's circuitry onto a wafer. The 6-inch mask standard dates back decades. It forces engineers to stitch together multiple exposures to build the enormous, transistor-dense dies that AI accelerators now need. Stitching adds cost. It adds defects too, and caps how big a single chip can get. A 12-inch mask, four times the area, removes a lot of that stitching requirement in one move. According to the ASML-TSMC announcement, that combination is expected to raise fab productivity and lower the cost per chip - which matters directly to a customer like Nvidia, buying tens of billions of dollars of wafers a year.

Why TSMC and Samsung Are Suddenly In

AS delegations head home from the 55th Pacific Islands Forum in Koror, capital of the Republic of Palau, the region's presidents, prime ministers and officials have endorsed a series of declarations and resolutions in their final communique.

Forum host and incoming chair, President of Palau Surangel Whipps Jr. said: "Over the week-long deliberations, we have reflected deeply on shared priorities. We affirmed our regional unity and agreed on clear actions to guide the Blue Pacific continent through an increasingly complex and challenging strategic environment...we acknowledge that we are in a very uncertain times with many competing priorities and contestation around us."

The summit agenda was overcrowded and bracketed by an extensive array of side-events, as crowds of dialogue partners, civil society groups and observers organised dozens of discussion panels and briefings. Despite the absence of six of the 18 elected leaders, country delegations grappled with the economic and energy implications of the US and Israel war on Iran and the challenge of finding sufficient resources to implement Forum development priorities.

The week's discussions came at a time of increasing strategic tensions between the United States and People's Republic of China, amplified by Canberra's "permanent competition" with Beijing and sharpening criticism of China by New Zealand. Throughout the week, much of the international media coverage highlighted debates about Taiwan, Chinese missile testing and US security agendas, often overshadowing Blue Pacific agendas on climate, oceans and human security.

The Forum communique contains the full details of the leaders' decisions, but here are some highlights on climate and oceans, nuclear challenges, the evolving reginal security architecture, and the challenge of engaging with an increasing number of partners.

Climate and oceans

Forum leaders issued a series of statements on climate action and the climate / oceans nexus, as members prepare for the opening of the UN General Assembly in September, October's pre-COP in Fiji and Tuvalu and then global climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

The "Palau Declaration for urgent and inclusive climate action to keep 1.5 within reach" sets out the region's climate agenda for the coming months, stressing "the urgency of ambitious global action consistent with the best available science". President Whipps noted that leaders also endorsed a Pacific Gender Climate Act "which represents our holistic commitment to gender responsive climate action."

Ad Forum chair, Whipps said that "we recognise that disasters continue to beset our region and the Pacific Humanitarian Response Coordination Mechanism operating guidelines we endorsed this week will give effect to a more structured regional response in times of humanitarian crisis."

It'll be fundamental grade school history one day, probably soon. This era will be How China Took Over Technology 101. China is simply blitzing the tech race on the ground.

To describe America's approach to basic business deployment in the tech sector as inept would be unmitigated flattery. It's so bad and so backward it barely needs describing, let alone explaining.

From a purely strategic perspective, a more precise description of the current situation over the last couple of years would be "America Gets Lost in its Own Closet". Big Tech isn't really calling the shots globally. Nothing like it, and it's beginning to show.

The perception of superior Western technology is rotting away nicely, too. China has been routinely catching up in all areas of tech deficiency, and the most that Big Tech can do is cling to advanced chip technologies like protective teddy bears.

China has gone around the chip embargos very easily and for a very simple reason. Adoption of new tech takes time. People simply don't need top of the line chips for most things. Routine daily business doesn't even begin to require that sort of advanced tech. Is your hot dog stand trying to compete with NASA? No? That sort of thing.

Very strange contrasts in how America and China do business

China's open source strategy is paying off. Open source is a good middle ground for any sort of tech and a reliable base for development. The US/China dichotomy doesn't have a role at the nuts-and-bolts level.

You can explore open source tech much more easily than proprietary tech. It's a classic case of hyper-possessive, expensive IP vs practical tech. Guess who's winning.

Chinese tech also comes with built-in support, hardware production, and working business models. It's on the ground now. America has produced a much resented and much more highly distrusted AI bubble, where gigantic amounts of capital are generating more press releases than solid business outcomes. This comes with corporate debt on a very strangely defined, evasive basis.

That last line should be a rhetorical statement. It isn't. There's an element of real pathos in the fact that much American investment is now transitioning to how to manage, implement, and deploy AI. This situation boils down to "Now we've got it, how do we make money out of it?"

China has done the exact opposite. The Chinese are fitting new tech to operational business needs using the more transparent open-source approach. The main obstacle seems to be how fast the customer base can respond.

Physical AI

Physical AI applies to robotics, real world interactions, and related hardware., This also just happens to be the intersection of high tech and real business. The Chinese have built a vast array of physical AI ready to ship.

Bloom Energy Corporation (NYSE:BE) jumped after trading on September 4 after it was announced that the stock had been added to the S&P 500, marking an important milestone for the company. The change will be effective prior to the open of trading on September 21, to coincide with the quarterly rebalance.

Bloom Energy has now surged by over 150% since the beginning of 2026, propelled by its growing role as a potential power provider for the booming AI data center industry. The fuel-cell power company had the strongest quarter in its history in Q2, easily exceeding expectations and delivering a revenue growth of over 166% compared to last year.

The strong demand for its power solutions also prompted Bloom to raise its full-year revenue outlook to the range of $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion, representing 100% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.

S&P 500 Inclusion Adds Fuel to Bloom's Rally:

The inclusion in the illustrious S&P 500 could increase Bloom Energy's exposure to institutional investors and generate additional demand from funds that track the benchmark. More importantly, the addition comes at a time when the company is gaining traction in the AI power market.

Bloom currently has an agreement with Oracle to supply the hyperscaler with up to 2.8 GW of fuel cell capacity, highlighting the value of its technology as data center operators seek power solutions that are quicker to deploy than conventional grid connections. Additionally, Bloom Energy also expanded its partnership with Brookfield Asset Management this summer, boosting their funding framework fivefold to $25 billion to accelerate the global deployment of the company's fuel cells.

Successfully converting these partnerships into large-scale deployments, and the addition of new ones, should continue to accelerate the growth of Bloom's revenue and cash flows.

S&P 500 Boost May Not Last:

While the inclusion in the S&P 500 could provide a temporary catalyst, Bloom Energy's long-term performance will ultimately depend on its underlying fundamentals. A high-growth narrative without a corresponding uptick in financial performance could expose the stock to a significant valuation correction.

The concerns of a potential AI bubble also present a significant risk. Hyperscalers are currently committing hundreds of billions of dollars to expand their data center capacity, but the long-term returns on these investments are still uncertain. Any meaningful slowdown in AI adoption, weaker-than-expected returns, or a subsequent pullback in capital spending could significantly weaken the projected power demand from data centers.
title: Bloom Energy (BE) Joins S&P 500: Can Its AI Rally Continue?

Mark Spitznagel, the Universa Investments founder who called the 2000 and 2008 crashes, says the S&P 500 has one more euphoric rally left in it before an 80% crash he compares to 1929. He expects the index to top 8,000 first, with the collapse arriving in the months ahead.

Mark Spitznagel called the 2000 and 2008 crashes. Now he says the S&P 500 has one more euphoric run left in it, past 8,000, before an 80% collapse he compares to 1929.

You've heard the AI bubble warnings all year. This one comes with a number attached. Mark Spitznagel, the founder of tail-risk hedge fund Universa Investments, told Business Insider in an email that he expects the S&P 500 to climb roughly 20% further, breaking through 8,000, before the market rolls over into what he calls the worst crash since 1929, with an eventual drawdown of 80%.

He's not guessing at a fresh thesis here. Spitznagel has been calling this a coming "blow-off" for more than three years, and he now says it should culminate "in the months ahead." "I've been looking for a blow-off in equities for over three years now, followed by the worst crash since 1929," he wrote. "That blow-off is still in process."

Here's the part that trips people up: Spitznagel isn't bearish right now. He calls himself "extremely bullish" on stocks through this final leg up, and Universa's entire strategy depends on staying invested in the rally while hedging the tail. It sounds like a contradiction. It isn't - it's the whole point of his fund. Universa buys deep out-of-the-money options that cost almost nothing in calm markets and pay off enormously when volatility spikes, which is why the firm posted a 4,144% return in the early weeks of the pandemic crash and has averaged triple-digit returns on that capital since 2007. You don't build a firm like that by predicting doom and sitting in cash. You build it by riding the euphoria and getting paid when the euphoria breaks.

Spitznagel isn't the only name attaching real numbers to this unease. Michael Burry disclosed a short position against Micron this year, calling the AI trade "just an asset bubble, plain and simple" even as the stock ran up nearly 700% over the past year. The CAPE ratio, a measure of how expensive stocks are relative to a decade of earnings, sat at 42.56 as of Burry's warning, within striking distance of its December 1999 record and more than double its 156-year average of 17. Frederick Neumann, HSBC's chief Asia economist, has drawn a different but related parallel, arguing that today's rising Treasury yields and AI-obsessed markets echo the setup before the 1997 Asian financial crisis, with South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Singapore now exposed through their dependence on US AI hardware demand rather than currency pegs.

Professor Park Jeong-ho analyzes AI labor shifts, space economy growth, and investment risks

Between August 24 and September 7, Park Jeong-ho, a special appointment professor at Myongji University's Practical Investment Analysis Department, appeared three times on the Chosun Ilbo's economic YouTube series "Chosun Money" to discuss the industrial restructuring in the upcoming era of AI humanoid robots and the dawn of the space economy.

Currently, U.S. Big Tech company Tesla is developing the humanoid robot "Optimus." Park compared Tesla's goal of producing 1 million Optimus units annually to "the equivalent of 1 million new American workers entering the labor force each year." He emphasized that robots will replace humans in service industries and manufacturing roles. "A world where expensive robots are rented and AI labor costs are paid in digital assets is coming," he said, diagnosing that the largest market in history is about to explode.

Park also dismissed the so-called "AI bubble theory" amid recent stock price declines, maintaining an optimistic outlook. He argued that while stock volatility is high because the path ahead is uncharted, real-world AI development and investment remain robust.

◇"Splinternet and China's 'Frog in a Pot' Strategy"

The global power struggle among the U.S., China, Russia, and Europe is fragmenting the internet into a "Splinternet" -- a term describing how the once-unified global network is splitting into isolated blocs aligned with national or ideological interests.

Park explained that China's insistence on developing its own operating systems and platforms stems from a philosophy of never surrendering "data ownership," the core of AI learning, to U.S. companies. He added that when personal AI agents autonomously make purchases, data and payment systems will likely become fully separated by nation.

He also likened China's weaponization of rare earth elements to the "frog in a pot" strategy -- gradually raising the heat until the frog is boiled. "China supplies cheap resources to its own companies while subtly controlling quantities and timing for competitors like South Korea and Japan, slowly eroding their profit margins," he analyzed.

Park further noted that U.S. Big Tech is pouring astronomical sums into small modular reactors (SMRs) and transparent solar panels to secure energy dominance. As this influx of capital destabilizes fiat currencies, investment banks are hedging against uncertainty by classifying Bitcoin as "digital gold."

◇"Space: The 21st-Century Middle East... SpaceX's $500 Space Delivery Revolution"

Park identified space as humanity's new frontier, comparing it to the Middle East during the oil boom. The revolution centers on SpaceX's reusable rocket technology, which slashed the cost of lifting 1 kilogram into orbit from $40,000 to just $500, ushering in the "space delivery" era.

"If only this could've been predicted," says the capitalist about the thing everyone warned him about.

Majority of CEOs Alarmed as AI Delivers No Financial Returns, They're worried they're not spending enough on AI.

By Victor Tangermann, Jan 21, 2026, Futurism

Investors continue to fret over an AI bubble "reckoning," as gains in productivity from the tech remain elusive.

According to a recent survey by professional services network PwC, more than half of the 4,454 CEO respondents said "their companies aren't yet seeing a financial return from investments in AI."

Only 30 percent reported increased revenue from AI in the last 12 months. However, a far more significant 56 percent said AI has failed to either boost revenue or lower costs. A mere 12 percent of CEOs reported that it'd accomplished both goals.

The findings once again underline lingering questions about the effectiveness of the tech. That's despite AI companies pouring tens of billions into data center buildouts and related infrastructure.

Instead of looking for other avenues for growth, though, PwC found that executives are worried about falling behind by not leaning into AI enough.

"A small group of companies are already turning AI into measurable financial returns, whilst many others are still struggling to move beyond pilots," said PwC global chairman Mohamed Kande in a statement. "That gap is starting to show up in confidence and competitiveness, and it will widen quickly for those that don't act."

PwC also pointed out that most companies were lacking the "AI foundations, such as clearly defined road maps and sufficient levels of investment" to realize a return.

But whether pouring even more money into AI will suddenly turn the tech into a money maker -- and not a major expense on the balance sheet -- remains the subject of a heated debate.

For now, the prognosis is still looking somewhat grim. Last year, a frequently-cited MIT report found that a staggering 95 percent of attempts to incorporate generative AI into business so far are failing to lead to "rapid revenue acceleration."

The effectiveness of the tech itself has also repeatedly been called into question, from frequent hallucinations and an inability to complete real-world office tasks to ongoing concerns over data security.

The topic of tangible returns on investment from AI is bound to be a major focus this year as executives wonder how to translate all that hype into real-world implementations -- and whether it'll actually help their bottom lines in the long run.

More on the AI hype: Terrified Investors Are Bracing for an AI Bubble "Reckoning"
title: Majority of CEOs Alarmed as AI Delivers No Financial Returns

Your Portfolio Is Likely Out of Balance

I'm a believer in setting an asset allocation target and sticking to it. That means reducing stocks when they have been hot and buying more when they turn cold. There is ample evidence that most investors do just the opposite: They get greedy and buy high, then panic and sell low. Because stocks have been surging since 2023, if you haven't rebalanced back to your target, you are likely way out of whack and aggressively invested.

Metrics Show Stocks Are Richly Valued by Historical Standards

Perhaps the most widely known valuation to predict the stock market is the S&P 500 Cyclically Adjusted Price-Earnings Ratio, which is calculated by dividing the current price of the S&P 500 by the 10-year moving average of its inflation-adjusted earnings. It was developed by Nobel Prize-winning economist Robert Shiller in 1988. The measure is nearing an all-time high, approaching the dot-com bubble of 2000. Other valuation methods, such as trailing PE, show similarly high valuations. And even firms like Vanguard are forecasting lower expected future equity returns. Admittedly, all of these metrics to predict future returns are based on history and back tested. They do a much better job of predicting the past than the future. Nonetheless, it is a warning sign.

Security Firms Show Investors Have Taken Out Record Margin Debt

Debit balances in customers' securities margin accounts are at record levels, rising from $1 trillion in June of 2025 to $1.5 trillion in June of 2026, according to FINRA. Investors borrow when they are brave in up markets but may panic and sell as the margins get closer to being called. Even if they don't panic, automated mass sales as margins are called could cause stocks to fall even further.

I'm Hearing Statements Like "Bonds Are for Cowards"

I'm also hearing people say things like "I want to be 100% in stocks," or "VTI and chill," referring to the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF. This means all one needs to do is put every penny of investments into a single fund and then be confident it will grow just like it has in the past. Allow me to make the case that the current administration, by design or by miscalculations, has put at risk the American economy, its national security and societal order. Readers of course may have their own opinions. Those may be manifest in the upcoming midterm elections.

The country is experiencing a wave of discontent with the administration from across the political spectrum. Forbes reported this past Monday the President's approval rating had dipped to 32%, and his disapproval rating had climbed to 64%. Further, Republican support had dropped 14% since April of this year. Reuters/Ipsos polling clocked in at 33% approval with disapproval also at 64%. CNN 32%/64%. Fox News reported 33%/64%.

For perspective, Joe Biden never dropped below 36%.

What are the people's concerns? They cover a range of issues and their order may have to do with Iran, income level, costs of food and energy, nature of business and farming, healthcare, or general financial anxiety.

WAR

Perhaps foremost in mind is the war with Iran. Several national polls have approval of Trump's handling of the war in the mid-20 percentages. Many of those polled react by saying that the war is taking money out of their pockets, with a large consensus saying that the war has increased the cost of gas and groceries. A UMass-Amherst poll this month indicated this to be true with 88% of Democrats, 77% of Independents, and 75% of Republicans. The forecast appears to be dark. These include a baseline of 10% on all imports and much higher rates on others like China and Canada. They have raised consumer costs. Although SpaceX rewrote Wall Street's record books with its $1.77 trillion IPO, which raised a record $85.7 billion, including the underwriters' overallotment, artificial intelligence (AI) start-up Anthropic aims to knock SpaceX from its pedestal.

The developer of the increasingly popular Claude large language model has already confidentially filed the necessary paperwork to go public and is widely expected to publish its registration statement (i.e., prospectus) after the Labor Day holiday. It's believed that Anthropic is seeking a late-September or early-October listing and a staggering $2 trillion valuation.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue "

While there's little doubt that retail investors will be lining up for their chance to buy into this hypergrowth opportunity, I won't be one of them. I'll be completely avoiding Anthropic's potentially record-breaking IPO for three historical reasons.

1. Tech-driven IPOs often stumble out of the starting gate

To begin with, tech-focused IPOs have been retail investor traps, more often than not, over the last 14 years.

In early June, before SpaceX went public, Truist Financial(NYSE:TFC) published the performance of the last 30 major tech-driven IPOs since mid-2012. Truist found that the average tech-focused IPO endured a year-one maximum drawdown of 55%! For context, SpaceX's all-time high-to-record-low drawdown is 54% thus far.

Truist's data set exposes the emotional aspect of IPO investing and the unsustainable nature of IPO buzz. While Anthropic was able to generate a small adjusted profit in the second quarter on more than $11.5 billion in sales, according to Bloomberg News, Anthropic's AI infrastructure build-out will cost a proverbial arm and a leg in the coming years and weigh heavily on its profit potential.

2. Anthropic's valuation is historically unsustainable

To state the obvious, valuing public companies involves some subjectivity, and there isn't a one-size-fits-all approach. Nevertheless, one historically unblemished valuation metric suggests that retail investors who pile into Anthropic early will regret it.

CMC Markets (LSE: CMCX) has quietly become one of the FTSE 250's standout performers, up more than 240% over the past year. That's no small feat, and for growth-focused UK investors, it warrants closer inspection.

But what exactly does the company do, and why has it suddenly captured investor imagination?

Piggybacking the AI trade

CMC Markets is a London-listed online trading and investing platform founded in 1989. It offers contracts for difference (CFDs), financial spread betting in the UK and Ireland, and stockbroking services across the UK, Australia, and Singapore.

The group serves retail, professional, and institutional clients in 12 countries, making money from:

* Spreads.

* Commissions.

* Overnight financing.

* Interest on client cash balances.

So how's a trading platform riding the AI wave?

Global equity markets have exploded higher on the back of surging demand for AI, particularly data centre infrastructure. Chipmakers and memory suppliers such as Nvidia, SanDisk, Western Digital, and Micron have seen their valuations soar as investors pile into anything AI-related.

While CMC Markets isn't building AI infrastructure, it's quietly benefiting from the trading frenzy around these names. The company's latest full-year results show net operating income up 15%, profit before tax up 20%, and a dividend of 13.8p.

Management highlighted record stockbroking activity in Australia and growing institutional partnerships as key drivers.In other words, as clients chase AI stocks and volatility picks up, CMC collects more spreads and commissions. But can this momentum last if AI enthusiasm fades?

Beyond the trading screen

Beyond offering access to AI stocks, CMC is sharpening its AI angle through content. Its Opto research arm regularly publishes pieces on AI themes and individual names, keeping clients engaged with the hottest topics in tech.

The platform relies on several types of complex tech systems, including:

* Advanced data processing.

* Algorithmic risk management.

* Automated pricing systems.

While these aren't inherently AI-driven, many of them increasingly benefit from AI enhancements.

But AI's still largely speculative, and CMC already faces key risks. Its earnings are cyclical, and heavily exposed to market volatility and client activity levels. Plus, CFDs and spread betting face tight regulation, with leverage caps and potential future restrictions.

Talk of a possible 'AI bubble' has been circling for months. If there is one, and it busts, a sharp correction could scare off retail clients, wiping out a chunk of CMC's user base.

This adds pressure to what is already a high valuation -- the price is almost 30 times earnings per
title: The AI trade is sending UK growth stock CMC Markets stratospheric -- is it still a buy?

TOKYO - Tokyo stocks fell sharply on September 8, with the Nikkei 225 closing at 65,269, down 1,130.51 points, or 1.70%, as a sudden surge in the yen hit exporters and forced investors to reassess the impact of faster Bank of Japan tightening on corporate earnings, equity valuations and the broader economy.

The broader TOPIX fell 75.47 points, or 1.83%, to 4,050.33, ending the recent resilience that had often seen it outperform the Nikkei during periods of AI and semiconductor volatility. The decline showed that the selloff was not limited to high-priced technology shares, with pressure spreading across exporters, financials, machinery, precision instruments and other sectors sensitive to currency and interest-rate moves.

The Nikkei gave back much of the previous day's 1,378-point rally, when chip and artificial intelligence-related shares had lifted the headline index despite weak market breadth. On September 8, the market moved in the opposite direction, as the yen's jump triggered broad selling and investors reduced exposure to shares that had benefited from the currency's weakness earlier in the summer.

The yen climbed as high as the 153 range against the dollar, its strongest level since February 18. The move was driven by an unwinding of short-yen and carry-trade positions as investors priced in faster BOJ tightening, supported by stronger wage data and an upward revision to Japan's April-June economic growth.

The currency move was the dominant force in Tokyo trading. A stronger yen helps reduce imported inflation pressure for households and companies, but it hurts exporters by lowering the yen value of overseas earnings. That weighed on automakers, machinery makers, precision-equipment companies and electronics shares.

Major exporters were sold as investors adjusted earnings assumptions. Toyota, Honda and other automakers had benefited from the dollar near 160 yen, but the move toward 153 sharply reduced that currency tailwind. The same pressure applied to machinery, electronic-component and precision-instrument makers with large overseas sales.

The speed of the yen's rise mattered as much as the level itself. A gradual move can be absorbed by markets, but a sharp currency swing forces investors to rebalance quickly, particularly after months in which weak-yen earnings expectations had supported Japanese equities.

The yen rally also changed the policy story. Until recently, markets were focused on whether Japanese authorities would intervene again to stop the yen from weakening beyond 160. On September 8, the issue shifted to whether the currency's rapid strengthening could become a new headwind for exporters and equity sentiment.

Nikkei CNBC-style market commentary would likely focus on the abrupt reversal in the market's leadership. The September 7 rally was driven by AI and semiconductor names, but September 8 showed that macro forces can quickly overwhelm sector-specific momentum when currency markets move sharply.

Every bank has bought copilots, agents and AI coding tools over the past two years, yet most large software transformations still take about as long as they did before.

Global banks have poured billions into foundation models, AI copilots and automated coding pipelines over the last few years, betting that generative AI would collapse the time and cost of large-scale software transformation. That bet has only partly paid off, AI can write code fast, but enterprise software estates are riddled with fragmented, undocumented dependencies that no model was trained to understand. Intellect Design Arena, a three-decade veteran of enterprise fintech, is positioning its newest product squarely at that gap rather than competing with the copilots banks have already bought.

Shares of Intellect Design Arena Ltd. were trading at Rs. 45.43, down 0.04 percent from previous close of Rs. 45.55. The stock opened at Rs. 45.47, reaching an intraday high of Rs. 45.77 and low of Rs. 45.27. The company currently has a market capitalization of Rs. 61,986 crores.

What's the News?

On September 8, 2026, Intellect Design Arena announced the launch of MSOCK - Multidimensional Multilayer System of Connected Knowledge - an AI-native enterprise knowledge system designed to make institutional knowledge connected, computable and visual for financial services. The company has filed 39 patents relating to the technology and will formally unveil it to the world on September 9, 2026, at the Global FinTech Fest in Mumbai, backed by a media push in a leading national business newspaper the same day.

At the core of MSOCK is a 21-dimensional Enterprise Spatial Graph that links business rules, processes, APIs and code into what Intellect calls Connected Knowledge Units, giving AI systems the architectural context to understand not just how to make a change but what it will affect. The company says it has already deployed MSOCK internally across more than 100 mission-critical projects, reporting cycle-time compression from 11-month projects down to 6 months and effort reduction from 170 person-months to 50 on validated engagements.

Financial & Business Analysis

Looking at the quarterly results of Intellect Design Arena Ltd., the company's consolidated revenue increased by 18.91 percent YoY, from Rs. 734.37 crore in Q1 FY26 to Rs. 873.23. crore in Q1 FY27, and decreased by 1.27 percent QoQ from Rs. 884.47 crore in Q4 FY26.

In Q1 FY27 Intellect Design Arena Ltd., consolidated net profit increased by 8.68 percent YoY, reaching Rs. 101.82 crore compared to Rs. 93.69 crore during the same period last year. As compared to Q4 FY26, the net profit has decreased by 15.31 percent, from Rs. 120.22 crore.

The basic earnings per share increased by 7.15 percent and stood at Rs. 7.34 as against Rs. 6.85 recorded in the same quarter in the previous year, FY2026.

The insurer's vendor-agnostic hub is already live in five entities, with AXA XL among those building claims and email applications

Transformation

By Mark Rosanes

Among insurers, the gap between those that have industrialised AI and those still running isolated pilots has widened materially in the past 12 months, according to research from Datos Insights published earlier this year, which found nearly 80% of large insurers have rolled out AI-assisted or autonomous processing workflows. AXA's partnership with Publicis Sapient is an example of what the industrialised end looks like. The agreement focuses on scaling AXA's Global AI Hub, a group-wide infrastructure layer for deploying and governing AI agents across the organisation.

AXA delivered its first platform version in July and it is already running across five entities. Among them is AXA XL, which places commercial lines, specialty and reinsurance risk for large corporates and institutions globally. The hub provides shared, standardised infrastructure for AI agents, with governance, compliance and human oversight built into the architecture.

What the hub actually does

AXA entities in Germany, France, Switzerland and the United Kingdom are developing applications including motor claims automation, customer email processing and enterprise knowledge management. The hub is designed to let individual entities develop on shared foundations rather than each independently building the same underlying infrastructure.

The hub is vendor-agnostic and supports multiple large language models across different use cases. That design reduces dependency on any single AI provider and allows AXA to switch or combine models as the technology evolves. Publicis Sapient provides the engineering and AI platform expertise to accelerate the build.

Matthieu Caillat, group chief technology and AI officer at AXA, said the priority was combining safe and efficient AI with governance and practical business applications. "Publicis Sapient brings together specialist AI expertise, enterprise AI solutions and global experience that will help us accelerate AI adoption consistently across our organisation, while maintaining the governance and flexibility required in a highly regulated business," he said.

Governance is the operational constraint

AXA has built governance into the hub's architecture from the start, rather than treating it as a compliance layer to add later. The hub embeds what AXA calls FinOps (cost management), SafetyOps (AI safety monitoring) and compliance oversight throughout the AI lifecycle.

The FCA has not introduced AI-specific rules, but the Consumer Duty and the Senior Managers and Certification Regime already apply to AI-assisted decisions. The Treasury Select Committee's January 2026 report noted that more than three-quarters of UK financial services firms already use AI for core functions, and called on the FCA to clarify how accountability under the SMCR operates where AI systems perform func
title: AXA scales governed AI infrastructure across global operations

India's enterprise AI investment rose 119% in one year, but only 22% of firms have proper AI governance systems in place.

India's enterprise AI investment soared 119 per cent in a year, surpassing the global average growth of 110 per cent, according to a report released on Tuesday.

The report by ServiceNow revealed that AI currently represents 16.6 per cent of the average IT budget in Indian enterprises and this share is expected to grow to 21.3 per cent by 2027.

Investment momentum is supported by India's robust digital public infrastructure, strong engineering talent, and rapid enterprise AI adoption rates.

Nevertheless, the report highlighted a significant gap in AI governance, with only 22 per cent of Indian enterprises having established testing, auditing, and risk assessment procedures.

While 54 per cent of Indian organisations have deployed AI agents, just 11 per cent have advanced to autonomous workflows.

Moreover, only 18 per cent of these organisations have replaced fragmented legacy systems with integrated platforms, meaning there is a lack of a unified layer for AI monitoring and governance.

Focus on Consequential Work

Kulmeet Bawa, Managing Director and Group Vice President of ServiceNow India and SAARC, stated, "India has proven it can commit to AI at a scale few markets can match. The next leap will be defined by how Indian enterprises pair that ambition with governance, connected data and workflows that let AI take on more consequential work."

He added that those organisations building solid governance foundations will unlock the next level of AI value in India.

India has proactively established an enabling framework through the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, DPDP Rules, and AI Governance Guidelines launched at the February 2026 AI Impact Summit.

The report also noted national initiatives like the IndiaAI Mission and the IndiaAI Safety Institute as evidence of a deliberate approach to AI governance.

Challenges remain with nearly 74 per cent of Indian enterprises identifying data accuracy, access, and management as major areas needing improvement, while 56 per cent cited legacy system integration as a significant hurdle.
title: India's Enterprise AI Investment Jumps 119%, Governance Measures Lag Behind
author: International Business Times, India Edition

content:
More than 75% of industrial AI pilot projects never reach large-scale deployment, and over 80% of manufacturers cannot extend AI beyond isolated use cases, according to a report by Everest Group and Capgemini Engineering -- with the failure attributed not to weak algorithms but to factory systems that cannot move data between each other.

The report, Operationalizing Adaptive AI Across the Manufacturing Shopfloor, was relayed by Moroccan business publication Challenge, which applied its findings to a country whose industrial base makes them unusually relevant.

The diagnosis

The obstacle, the report argues, is architectural. In many factories, IT systems including ERP and PLM platforms operate separately from OT environments -- MES, SCADA, controllers and production equipment -- leaving data poorly connected or arriving too late to support automated decisions.

Nicolas Rousseau, head of engineering technologies at Capgemini Engineering, put it plainly: digital ambition is not the constraint in manufacturing today. Execution is.

Four obstacles are identified: rigid processes, legacy technology, fragmented data and a shortage of cross-functional skills.

That diagnosis will be familiar. PwC's survey of South African mining found more than 85% of respondents rating their data management capabilities average or poor, with one chief executive observing that "data doesn't help if it's just data. It needs to be put through the funnel to get to wisdom." Nearly 70% of mines rated their AI readiness poor or very poor, and identified skills rather than technology as the binding constraint.

Different sector, different country, same conclusion.

Infrastructure first, applications second

The report's prescription reverses the usual sequence. Rather than starting with algorithms, it recommends manufacturers first build architecture capable of connecting equipment and structuring data -- through a Unified Namespace, the MQTT protocol for local connectivity, and in some cases streaming platforms such as Kafka. The rollout can be progressive, starting with a single production line before expanding.

Hybrid edge-cloud architecture is the second element, processing data close to equipment to cut latency and reduce dependence on constant cloud connectivity. Challenge argues this suits Moroccan manufacturers working with ageing infrastructure and technical debt -- outdated data formats and proprietary protocols.

The report also warns against rushing to full automation. With nearly half of manufacturers still struggling to integrate IT and OT, deploying autonomous agents onto ageing infrastructure risks adding complexity rather than removing it.

As operational systems open toward cloud and AI applications, cybersecurity and compliance become part of the architecture rather than an afterthought -- a point Challenge notes carries weight for Moroccan manufacturers handling sensitive data for international clients, alongside growing interest in sovereign AI offerings
title: Three-Quarters of Industrial AI Pilots Never Scale. The Problem Is Plumbing, Not Algorithms. - iAfrica.com

It called on the FCA to clarify how accountability under the SMCR operates where AI systems perform functions traditionally subject to direct human oversight. The hub's human oversight component addresses that question at the infrastructure level, though how it functions in practice is not yet pu

content:
Indian AI investment surged significantly, outpacing global growth rates. However, widespread AI readiness and risk assessment processes remain underdeveloped. Many companies deploy AI agents but hesitate with autonomous workflows due to transparency concerns. Fragmented legacy systems and data management issues hinder AI integration and maturity.

Enterprise AI investment in India grew 119% in the past year, ahead of the 110% global growth, according to the ServiceNow Enterprise AI Maturity Index 2026. Artificial intelligence (AI) now accounts for 16.6% of the average IT budget of Indian companies and is expected to rise to 21.3% by 2027.

However, the rapid spending is not translating into widespread AI readiness.

Only 22% of Indian enterprises have processes in place for testing, auditing and assessing AI-related risks, the report said. At the same time, 54% of organisations are deploying AI agents, while just 11% have moved to autonomous workflows.

The gap points to a growing caution among Indian businesses around letting AI act independently, particularly as agents get access to company data, systems and decision-making processes.

Also Read: AI in Indian healthcare still stuck in pilots, but the scale-up opportunity is growing: Bain, HealthQuad

Transparency and the risk of misinformation are the biggest concerns, cited by 60% of organisations. Regulatory and compliance complexity follows at 55%, while 50% flagged data privacy and security.

"India has proven it can commit to AI at a scale few markets can match. The next leap will be defined by how Indian enterprises pair that ambition with governance, connected data and workflows that let AI take on more consequential work," said Kulmeet Bawa, managing director and group vice president, ServiceNow India and SAARC.

The technology infrastructure underneath AI is another weak spot as only 18% of Indian organisations have replaced fragmented legacy systems with an integrated platform, while AI-enabled workflows scored just 41 out of 100 in the study. About 74% of organisations said data accuracy, access and management need to be strengthened for AI, while 56% pointed to legacy system integration.

This has left India with an overall AI governance score of 55 out of 100, well below the 78 scored by APAC's AI Pacesetters.

This is important because the more mature AI adopters are already seeing significant returns. APAC Pacesetters are generating a 149% return on investment from AI, which is expected to rise to 181% over the next two years. They are also six times more productive than their peers, according to the report.

For Indian companies, the next phase of AI adoption could therefore be less about simply deploying more models and more about connecting the systems, data and workflows that allow AI to take on more complex work.

Ashvin Vellody, partner and chief strategy and innovation officer
title: India's AI spend set to cross 21% of IT budgets by 2027: ServiceNow

Dear Baron Durable Advantage Fund Shareholder,

Performance

We had an OK quarter.

Baron Durable Advantage Fund (the Fund) gained 13.6% (Institutional Shares) during the second quarter, compared to the 15.2% gain for the S&P 500 Index (the Index), the Fund's benchmark.

Year to date, the Fund is up 3.4%, compared to the 10.2% gain for the Index.

We wrote in the last quarterly letter how the first quarter of 2026 had many similarities to the first quarter of 2025. We were coming off of multiple years of strong market returns buoyed by a strong economy and optimism about the AI buildout, with the Fund performing exceedingly well, and it "felt" like we were due for a "breather". Obviously, those things are impossible to predict so we don't even try, but we are fond of reminding ourselves that your prospective returns are negatively correlated to the recent ones, and when you have done this long enough, there are times when it's just... in the air. The market is looking for an excuse to consolidate or for an outright pullback. In the first quarter of last year, we got the "tariff tantrum" in mid-February and experienced an approximately 15% drawdown over the next seven weeks, with the Fund posting a 7.0% decline for its March 2025 quarter. This year, we were once again coming off of multiple years of strong returns (23.0% 3-year annualized return for the Index, and 29.2% for the Fund) buoyed by a strong economy and optimism about the AI buildout, and we got the Iran war and $140 oil. The Fund lost 9.0% for the March 2026 quarter. In the second quarter of last year the market staged a nice recovery with a gain of 10.9% for the Index, while the Fund was up 15.6%. It's not like tariffs went away or trade deals were finalized, but some tariffs were postponed, some compromises were agreed to, the worst outcomes were avoided, and investors figured it's unlikely to have a material long-term impact on the market. Entering this quarter, we speculated that something similar was likely to happen because past history (including recent examples of Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Middle East-Iran) suggested that geopolitical events have minimal lasting impact on equity markets. This is basically how it played out. It's not like there was a regime change in Iran, or a peace treaty was signed, but there was a Memorandum of Understanding, and ships resumed transiting the Strait of Hormuz (sort of...), oil pulled back to $70, and the worst outcomes seemed to have been avoided. New Delhi: India's enterprise AI investment surged 119 per cent in a single year above the global average of 110 per cent, yet only 22 per cent of Indian enterprises have testing, auditing and risk‑assessment processes in place, a report said on Tuesday.

The report from ServiceNow said that AI now accounts for 16.6 per cent of India's average IT budget and is projected to rise to 21.3 per cent by 2027.

The report noted that investment momentum in India is being built on world-class digital public infrastructure, deep engineering talent and one of the fastest rates of enterprise AI adoption globally.

However, the next phase will depend more on how confidently companies can govern AI. The gap is already visible as 54 per cent of Indian organisations are deploying AI agents, but only 11 per cent have moved to autonomous workflows.

Only 18 per cent of Indian organisations have replaced fragmented legacy systems with an integrated platform, the firm said, adding that there is no single layer through which AI can be monitored, audited or governed.

"India has proven it can commit to AI at a scale few markets can match. The next leap will be defined by how Indian enterprises pair that ambition with governance, connected data and workflows that let AI take on more consequential work," said Kulmeet Bawa, Managing Director & Group Vice President, ServiceNow India and SAARC.

The organisations that build these foundations first, will unlock AI's next tier of value for India, Bawa added.

India has moved early to put an enabling framework in place -- from the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the DPDP Rules, to the AI Governance Guidelines launched at the February 2026 AI Impact Summit.

Further, the IndiaAI Mission, and the establishment of the IndiaAI Safety Institute indicates a purposeful national approach to AI, the report noted.

Nearly 74 per cent Indian enterprises flagged data accuracy, access and management as the area most in need of strengthening for AI, and 56 per cent pointed to legacy system integration.
